title: 3-Read Friday #113: AI that supports learning, fact fluency, and doesn't teach fractions!
author: Craig Barton
summary: Craig Barton's 3-Read Friday #113 selects three pieces for the week, two of them maths-heavy by his own admission. Ethan Mollick's 'Choosing to Stay Human' explores a central tension in AI and education: AI undermines learning when it lets students surrender the hard cognitive work that learning requires, making the central design task for educators building AI use that pushes learners to think rather than think for them. Dylan Kane's 'Incremental Fact Fluency v2' argues that breaking math facts into incremental fact families, practiced in isolation and then interleaved and supported by relational strategies, is a viable path to fluency for reluctant students. Dan Murphy's 'Don't Teach Fractions. Not Yet' argues that fractions make sense to students only after a deep grounding in ratios, using precise language and a concrete-to-abstract progression that mirrors how mathematics and children's understanding actually develop. Barton notes this is an AI-heavy and maths-heavy week, and all three pieces share a concern with sequencing and cognitive readiness.
points: Mollick's core argument — that AI undermines learning when it does the hard cognitive work for students — is the central design challenge for any educator integrating AI: the tool must push learners to think, not think for them.

Kane's incremental fact fluency approach breaks from typical instruction by isolating fact families before interleaving them and backing each with relational strategies and explicit teaching, giving reluctant students a structured path to fluency.

Murphy's case against teaching fractions before ratios challenges standard curriculum sequencing, arguing the conceptual grounding students need to make sense of fractions comes from ratios, not the reverse.
All three pieces are united by a concern for instructional sequence and cognitive readiness: when and in what order ideas are introduced matters as much as how they are taught.
quotes: Podcast listeners will know that I am in the midst of a mini-series on AI in education, and one of the key tensions between my guests has been their views on whether giving students access to an AI in various forms will support or hinder their learning.

Here, Ethan argues that AI undermines learning when it lets students surrender the hard cognitive work that learning requires, so the central task for educators is designing AI use that pushes learners to think rather than think for them.

Dylan argues that breaking math facts into incremental fact families, practised in isolation, then interleaved, supported by relational strategies and careful teaching, is a viable way to get reluctant students enough practice to reach fluency... and he shares his resources!

Dan argues that fractions make sense to students only when taught after a deep grounding in ratios, using precise language and a concrete-to-abstract progression that mirrors how mathematics--and children's understanding--actually develops
Fractions are where math stops making sense for many kids. Not because they're hard. Because we teach them backwards.
Euclid spent four books on ratios. He never wrote a fraction. That's not an oversight but a roadmap we've ignored.
Fractions express parts of unity or one (1). Ratios express a relationship between two natural numbers. Fractions require introducing a new kind of number (rational numbers) into the child’s world.
